messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
The Cantor Intersection Theorem establishes the equivalence between completeness and the finite intersection property for nested closed sets. A metric space $(M, d)$ is complete if every Cauchy sequence in $M$ converges to a point within $M$. Conversely, if the space is not complete, there exists a Cauchy sequence that does not converge, which can be used to construct a counterexample to the intersection property.

To prove the forward direction, assume $(M, d)$ is complete and let $\{F_n\}$ be a sequence of nonempty closed subsets such that $F_{n+1} \subset F_n$ and $\text{diam}(F_n) \to 0$. Select a point $x_n \in F_n$ for each $n$. Since $F_{n+1} \subset F_n$, the distance between any two points $x_m, x_n$ with $m > n$ is bounded by $\text{diam}(F_n)$. Because the diameter tends to zero, the sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy. By completeness, there exists a limit point $x \in M$ such that $x_n \to x$. For any fixed $k$, all terms $x_n$ with $n \ge k$ lie in $F_k$. Since $F_k$ is closed and contains the tail of the sequence, it must contain the limit $x$. Therefore, $x$ belongs to every $F_n$, implying $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty F_n \neq \emptyset$.

To prove the reverse direction, assume that any such nested sequence of nonempty closed sets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. Let $(x_n)$ be an arbitrary Cauchy sequence in $M$. Define $F_n = \overline{\{x_k : k \ge n\}}$, the closure of the tail of the sequence. Each $F_n$ is closed and nonempty. The nesting condition $F_{n+1} \subset F_n$ holds because the tail starting at $n+1$ is a subset of the tail starting at $n$. Furthermore, since $(x_n)$ is Cauchy, for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $N$ such that $d(x_i, x_j) < \epsilon$ for all $i, j \ge N$. This implies $\text{diam}(F_N) \le \epsilon$, so $\text{diam}(F_n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. By the hypothesis, there exists a point $x \in \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty F_n$. Since $x \in F_n$ for all $n$, and $d(x, x_n) \le \text{diam}(F_n)$, it follows that $d(x, x_n) \to 0$. Thus, the Cauchy sequence converges to $x$, proving that $M$ is complete.
